title: Shaking Hands and Other Gracious Acts
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece uses Jimmy Carter's decades-long habit of personally shaking hands with everyone on his commercial flights as an example of how leaders can use their status or intangible assets to make others feel valued. The author frames this as an act of grace available to any leader with some form of standing, relationship, influence, or experience — not just former presidents. It offers everyday parallels: publicly crediting others' contributions, using relationships to introduce a team member to an influential person, or extending access to special privileges. The essay closes by challenging readers to actually use whatever assets they have this way, framing the choice as a test of character rather than capability.
points: Jimmy Carter spent nearly 50 years personally shaking hands with everyone on his commercial flights after his presidency.
The gesture illustrates how leaders can use status, relationships, or influence — not just skills — to make others feel valued.
Everyday parallels include publicly crediting others, sharing relationships, or extending access to special privileges.
Small, genuine gestures grounded in true compassion carry outsized impact.
The piece frames using one's assets this way as a matter of will, not capability — 'the only question is will you.'
quotes: Before he took his seat, Carter would shake hands with everyone on board.
The grace in that simple act touched many people in the nearly 50 years he made a habit of this magnanimous gesture.
Anytime a leader uses their position, their skills, or their qualities to make others feel special and appreciated, they act with grace.
Simple gestures can go a long way to move people if they are thoughtful and genuine.
Using those resources to make others feel valued comes from true compassion and grace.
